## Install

```{r, eval = FALSE}
# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("joonho112/regdatasets")

# A fixed release keeps every number in a course stable:
remotes::install_github("joonho112/regdatasets@v1.0.0")
```

## Find a dataset

`list_datasets()` lists every dataset with its size and the regression topics
it suits:

```{r}
library(regdatasets)
datasets <- list_datasets()
datasets[, c("dataset", "rows", "cols", "topics")]
```

Filter by topic to find data for a particular method:

```{r}
list_datasets(topic = "ordinal")[, c("dataset", "title")]
```

## Understand the variables

Every dataset has a help page, for example `?gcse`. The variable table on that
page is also available as a data frame through `codebook()`, which hides empty
columns when printed so value meanings stay readable. For wide datasets, filter
by `label` or `group`, or inspect interactively with `View(codebook("nels_data"))`:

```{r}
codebook("gcse")[, c("variable", "label", "values", "units")]
```

```{r}
cb <- codebook("nels_data")
nrow(cb)
cb[
  grepl("locus of control", cb$label, ignore.case = TRUE),
  c("variable", "label", "group")
]
```

## Use the data

The datasets are loaded on first use; no `data()` call is needed. They are
plain tibbles without attached Stata labels: most variables are numeric
(`integer` or `double`), seven datasets include `character` columns (such as
`titanic$embarked` or `reading$group`), and `disc$race` / `disc2$race` are
factors. Value meanings are always documented in `codebook()` and the help page.

```{r}
head(gcse)
```

### Categorical variables and `factor()`

Because multi-level survey codes are kept as integers (for example
`titanic$pclass`, `individuals$job`, or `berkeley$department`), wrap them in
`factor()` inside model formulas so R creates dummy indicators rather than
fitting a linear trend across arbitrary code numbers. Use `relevel()` to change
the reference category of a factor (for example
`relevel(disc$race, ref = "White")`). Also check binary codings in `codebook()`:
most indicators are `0/1`, while several survey items (such as
`individuals$sex` or `nels_data$bys74`) keep their original `1/2` coding and
must be recoded to `0/1` (for example `I(bys74 == 2)`) before passing them as
the outcome of `glm(..., family = binomial)`.

### First models

A first linear regression, with the reading test at age 11 predicting the
exam score at age 16:

```{r}
fit <- lm(gcse ~ lrt, data = gcse)
coef(summary(fit))
plot(
  gcse ~ lrt,
  data = gcse,
  pch = 16,
  col = grDevices::adjustcolor("grey30", 0.2),
  xlab = "London Reading Test (age 11)",
  ylab = "GCSE score (age 16)"
)
abline(fit, lwd = 2)
```

A logistic regression of Titanic survival:

```{r}
fit2 <- glm(
  survived ~ factor(pclass) + sex + age,
  data = titanic,
  family = binomial
)
round(exp(coef(fit2)), 2)   # odds ratios
```

## Missing values

Survey nonresponse codes such as "8 = missing" or "99.98" were recoded to
`NA` in version 1.0.0, so they can no longer enter a model as if they were
real values. `codebook()` shows, for each variable, what was recoded:

```{r}
cb <- codebook("nels_data")
cb[
  cb$variable %in% c("byses", "f1locus1"),
  c("variable", "na_count", "recoded_to_na")
]
```

## Where the data come from

Each help page ends with a **Source** section. `LICENSE.note` lists the source
of every dataset, how it reached this package and why it may be
redistributed. The article *How the data are built* on the package website
describes the reproducible build.
